reran: cmd.sh on w4-int, w3-base and 2.13.18 (scalac/scala through coursier): identical to actual.txt, K, L and V have no annotation in the joint build and A(classOf[...]) in the separate one. My variant on w4-int: @B(value = {String.class, int[].class}, name = "n") @Deprecated on a class and on methods, in both orders, with String[][].class and Map.Entry[].class: only the annotation holding the primitive or array class literal is dropped, its sibling @Deprecated is kept (same four deprecation warnings joint and separate), and nothing fails to parse.
user_impact: scalac's own checks lose nothing: the Java annotations it reads from source (@Deprecated, and @Retention, @Target, @Repeatable, @Inherited on annotation definitions) never take a primitive or array class literal; @FunctionalInterface, @SafeVarargs and nullability annotations have no effect in Scala 2 and take no class arguments. Run-time reflection, Java or Scala, reads javac's class files and sees the annotation. What is lost is the compile-time view in a mixed build: a macro or compiler plugin that inspects a Java symbol's annotations (for example a serialization macro reading @JsonDeserialize(as = int[].class)) sees the annotation in a separate build and not in a joint one; such arguments are uncommon.
fixability: clear cut, as part of GJ3's fix: JLS 9.7.1 allows only constant expressions, class literals (including primitive, void and array ones), enum constants, annotations and array initializers as element values, so an elementValue that parses constant expressions with constantExprOpt (stopping at `,`, `)` and `}`) and class literals with the type parser (`typ()` then `.class`) handles every valid argument, leaving the bail-out unreachable for valid Java. Cost: joint builds see annotations separate builds already see.
regression: no (JavaParsers has parsed annotation arguments since scala/scala PR 5892, first in 2.12.12 and 2.13.3; before that these annotations were not read from source at all; 2.13.18 is the same)
links: GJ3 (retronym/scala PR 757, test only) and J5 (retronym/scala PR 288): the same bail-out in JavaParsers.annotation, three triggers of it (operator expression, parenthesis, primitive or array class literal). One pull request should fix all three: extend 757 with WJ1's cases (it already sketches class literals, but only reference ones go through qualId today) and let it replace 288, whose change only makes the skip land on the right parenthesis and still drops the annotation. R5 (retronym/scala PR 313) concerns the same String[].class literal in run-time reflection, a different cause.
note: The detail's mechanism is right (elementValue returns EmptyTree for a primitive keyword token; qualId stops at `[` after String) and the parser recovers cleanly, so the symptom is only the missing annotation. The hunter's claim that 757's write-up does not cover this is half right: its sketch says class literals but would need the type parser to cover primitive, void and array ones; the fix belongs in the same pull request, not a separate one.
